metadata.title: Every Reading Said Fine
metadata.note: STEM explainer built on my own real-time-vitals-pipeline repo. The one idea: a measurement carries no direction, so a deteriorating patient is invisible to any single reading. Every figure was computed in this session by running the repo's own simulator and MEWS scorer over 1,800 readings, not taken from its README. B02 is the project's actual interface rather than an illustration of it.

beats.narration: Hi, I am Kehinde Obidele and this video is about a patient who was quietly failing while almost every single reading said they were fine. I built a streaming pipeline that watches bedside vitals, and the number that stayed with me is 62 percent.

props.command: I ran my vitals pipeline over 1,800 readings from one deteriorating patient. Their oxygen saturation fell 18 points. 62 percent of the individual readings still scored as normal. Help me explain why a single reading cannot see this, and what does.
output: the drift is the finding, not the reading

beats.new_visual_element: Hesitant writer, the assumption corrected on screen
beats.narration: I assumed a deteriorating patient would show up in a reading. They do not. A reading tells you where someone is. It cannot tell you which way they are going.

beats.new_visual_element: My own telemetry wall, twelve patients at once
beats.narration: This is the front end I built for it. Twelve patients, one reading per second, each tile carrying a synthesized trace that sweeps at that patient's own heart rate. The small five-spoke glyph on each tile is the warning score: one spoke per measured parameter, one notch per point. A bare centre is a well patient. You can read a whole ward from the glyphs without reading a single number.

beats.new_visual_element: Two rules: score the reading, then watch the patient
beats.narration: Two rules do the work. The first scores a single reading: each parameter gets nought to three points against published bands, and you add them up. Five or more means immediate review. The second compares a reading against that patient's own rolling average, in units of their own variability, and flags anything more than three standard deviations out.

beats.new_visual_element: Most readings looked normal the whole way down
beats.narration: Here is what happened over 1,800 readings from one patient in respiratory failure. Oxygen saturation fell from 98 to 80, eighteen points. Breathing rate nearly doubled. And 62 percent of those readings still scored two or below, which reads as normal. Only 1.3 percent ever crossed the immediate-review threshold on their own. The patient was failing the whole time and most individual readings said otherwise.

props.headline: What the individual readings said
props.subhead: Scored one by one, as a bedside check would.
props.footnote: Same patient. Same window. The deterioration was real throughout.

beats.new_visual_element: Five consecutive readings moving one way
beats.narration: So the pipeline does not only score readings. It also watches their direction. If five or more consecutive readings move the same way, that is flagged as sustained drift, regardless of whether any one of them is abnormal. That rule exists precisely because no single reading was abnormal. Direction is information that a measurement does not carry on its own.

resolver.label: DIRECTION, NOT VALUE
resolver.detail: A measurement has no direction. Five of them do.

beats.narration: One design decision I would defend. This data is continuous bedside telemetry, so I built the interface out of that shape rather than pouring it into default charts. The trace refreshes with a moving erase bar, the way a real monitor does, not as a scrolling window. Colours follow real monitor convention. A clinician should not have to learn a new visual language to read it.

beats.new_visual_element: What a ward of readings taught me
beats.narration: The honest summary is that this is the same lesson as my textbook work, in a different domain. A fact that was true when it was taken is not true now, and checking it once tells you nothing about the direction it was already moving in.

artifactLines: A measurement has no direction. A sequence does.
Most readings looked normal the whole way down.
Scoring each reading well is not the same as watching the patient.
An alert on every bad reading is an alarm nobody answers.
Ask what a value was doing, not only what it is.

beats.new_visual_element: The viewer gets the same job
beats.narration: So here is what I would hand to you. Take a number you check regularly, at work or anywhere else, and instead of asking whether today's value is acceptable, line up the last five and ask which way they are pointing. That question catches things no single check will.
